title: Fever in Adults Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing fever, identifying serious infections, sepsis risk, and source of fever to guide investigation and safe management.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, sepsis protocols or urgent escalation when serious infection is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Sepsis or septic shock (fever with suspected infection source, systemic illness, hypotension).
Meningitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness).
Pneumonia (fever, cough, focal chest signs, hypoxia).
Urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis (dysuria, fever, flank pain).
Endocarditis (fever, murmur, malaise, emboli signs).
Intra-abdominal infection (fever with abdominal tenderness, peritoneal signs).
Source of fever if high or prolonged (malignancy, TB, autoimmune).
Immunosuppression increasing infection risk or atypical presentation.
items.importantLimitation: Absence of obvious source does not exclude serious infection. Some serious infections present with fever alone.

items.title: Fever pattern and characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; duration.
Height: peak temperature; pattern (constant, intermittent, spiking)?
Associated: chills, rigors, night sweats, diaphoresis.
Preceding illness: URI, gastroenteritis, other infection.
Travel history or unusual exposures.

items.title: Symptoms suggesting source
mustConfirmOrExclude: Respiratory: cough, sputum, dyspnoea, pleurisy.
Urinary: dysuria, frequency, urgency, flank pain.
GI: diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rigidity.
CNS: headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness.
Skin: rash, wound infection, cellulitis.
Cardiac: murmur history, prosthetic valve, recent procedure.

items.title: Systemic illness and red flags
mustConfirmOrExclude: Malaise, fatigue, myalgia, headache.
Confusion or altered consciousness.
Tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnoea (sepsis signs).
Hypoxia or respiratory distress.
Rash: maculopapular, petechial, or purpuric?
Recent surgery, instrumentation, or procedural risk.

items.title: Sepsis or septic shock
urgentFeatures: Fever with suspected infection and systemic illness.
Hypotension, signs of hypoperfusion or oliguria.
implications: Emergency assessment; sepsis protocol activation (antibiotics, fluids, lactate monitoring).

items.title: Meningitis
urgentFeatures: Fever with headache and neck stiffness.
implications: Emergency referral; empiric antibiotics if suspected.

items.title: Community-acquired pneumonia
urgentFeatures: Fever with cough, dyspnoea, focal chest signs.
CRP >100 or focal infiltrate on imaging.
implications: Chest X-ray; antibiotics and hospital referral if severe.

items.title: Vital signs and general assessment
howToTest: Temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation.
General appearance: well, unwell, toxic, confused.
Skin: colour, perfusion, rash type and distribution.
normal: Fever with normal or minimally abnormal vital signs otherwise.
abnormal: Tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnoea, hypoxia, altered appearance, purpuric/petechial rash.
implications: Abnormal vital signs with fever suggest systemic infection.

items.title: Organ system examination
howToTest: Respiratory: breath sounds, crackles, consolidation signs.
Cardiac: murmurs, prosthetic sounds, signs of endocarditis.
Neuro: meningeal signs, focal deficits, consciousness.
Skin: wounds, cellulitis, purpura, splinter haemorrhages.
abnormal: Focal signs suggesting infection source (respiratory, abdominal, cardiac, CNS, skin).
implications: Focal findings guide investigation and antibiotic choice.

items.title: Viral infection
commonFindings: Fever with URI/flu symptoms, malaise, myalgia.
No focal signs or mild findings.
implications: Supportive care; no antibiotics for viral infection.

items.title: UTI or pyelonephritis
commonFindings: Flank pain or CVA tenderness in pyelonephritis.
Positive urine dipstick; pyuria on microscopy.

items.title: Respiratory tract infection
implications: Chest imaging; antibiotics if bacterial pneumonia suspected.

items.title: Investigation
mustConfirmOrExclude: FBC, CRP, blood cultures if fever >38.5°C or high sepsis risk.
Urinalysis and urine culture if UTI suspected.
Chest X-ray if respiratory symptoms.
Consider LP if meningitis suspected (after CT if needed).

items.title: Community management when
mustConfirmOrExclude: Low-risk appearance and vital signs.
Fever <38.5°C or resolving trend.
Likely viral illness; no focal serious features.

items.title: Urgent hospital referral
urgentFeatures: Signs of sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status).
Fever with meningeal signs, focal neurological signs, or petechial rash.
Fever with respiratory distress or hypoxia.

items.title: Fever in adults
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: fever with signs of sepsis (severe illness, confusion, difficulty breathing); fever with meningeal signs (headache, neck stiffness, rash); or fever with signs of shock.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: high fever (>39°C) with severe systemic illness; fever with focal infection signs (dysuria, chest pain, abdominal tenderness); fever lasting >7 days without clear source; or worsening fever despite paracetamol.
Speak to your GP if: fever is resolving but you want antibiotic advice; you want investigation of prolonged fever; or you are concerned about underlying causes.
